> Across two studies, participants were told that they would receive either a high-, low-or very-low-calorie dinner later during the day -the food EFT (vs control not related to food).

> 131 participants were recruited via the departmental participant pool, the staff community board and private communication at Swansea University.

> Based on these exclusion criteria, data from seven participants had to be excluded (1 was vegetarian, 3 guessed the aim, and 3 had a BMI (Body Mass Index) < 18kg/m 2 ), which left data from 124 participants for analyses.

> The study was approved by the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Swansea University, informed consent was obtained, and pre-registered at the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/pydvz/; DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PYDVZ).

> The study followed a between subject design and participants were randomly allocated to the experimental or control condition (block randomisation of 10 participants per block using http://www.random.org/).

> Participants were presented with a range of snacks and were instructed to rate the sweetness, saltiness, bitterness, sourness, crunchiness, softness, liking, and healthiness of each food on a 100mm Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) to distract from the real aim of assessing intake (sensory data not otherwise used in the analysis).

> Participants were invited to the study between 14.00 and 18.30 to increase consistency and the likelihood that they had eaten lunch but not dinner (similar to e.g., Higgs et al., 2008).

> As can be seen in Table 1, comparable numbers of participants were in the control and experimental condition (49.2% vs 50.8%, respectively), with a similar distribution of female and male participants.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: 131 participants were recruited via the departmental participant pool, the staff community board and private communication at Swansea University. Exclusion criteria were an age under 18 years and a BMI under 18 kg/m 2, as well as food allergies or intolerances, a history of or a current diagnosed eating disorder, medications or medical conditions influencing appetite and/or taste perception, low English proficiency, being currently pregnant or breast feeding, guessing the true aim of the study, and having taken part in a previous study by the researchers. Based on these exclusion criteria, data from seven participants had to be excluded (1 was vegetarian, 3 guessed the aim, and 3 had a BMI (Body Mass Index) < 18kg/m 2 ), which left data from 124 participants for analyses. This exceeded the 114 participants needed based on an a-priori sample size calculations in G*Power (Faul et al., 2009): multiple linear regression model with α-error probability of 0.05, statistical power of 0.8, three predictors (manipulation as predictor, restraint as moderator, and the interaction) and a small to medium effect size of f² = 0.1 (based on Price et al., 2016).

In total, 3 participants had to be excluded (1 guessed the exact aim and 2 had a BMI < 18 kg/mfoot_2 ) leaving data of 187 participants for analyses. According to the a-priori sample size calculation based on an ANCOVA in G*Power (Faul et al., 2009), 146 participants would have been needed to get a power of 0.8 with an effect size of 0.26 (based on study 1), numerator df=2, α-error=0.05, covariates=9, and number of groups=3.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Association between prospective memory of eating plans and snack intake, and influence of personality and trait tendencies to plan indulgence on this association
table.research_questions:
We want to investigate the association between priming of prospective memory for eating plans and opportunistic snack intake and the possible effects of personality traits and trait tendencies to plan indulgences. 

1. Confirmatory analysis: 
In a moderation analysis we want to investigate the association between priming of participants to think about eating plans for the rest of the day and intake, and if trait tendencies to plan indulgences moderates this interaction. We will take following possible covariates into account: eating traits (DEBQ, flexible and rigid restraint sub-scales, craving, impulsiveness), time perspective, age, gender, BMI, hunger, liking, desire to eat, perceived healthiness and mood (PANAS). First, we will correlate them with intake and only use variable as covariates which are significantly correlated with intake,

2. Exploratory analysis: 
a. In an exploratory moderation analysis, we are also interested if time perspective, impulsiveness and restrained eating moderate the association between the priming and intake, as well as the moderation by trait tendencies to plan indulgences while taking a series of covariates into account. We will take the same covariates as in the confirmatory analysis into account and follow the same procedure.
b. Additionally, we want to investigate possible influences of personality and eating traits on the perceived effectiveness of planning indulgence to reduce intake of snacks. 
c. During initial testing of the wording of the priming, participants did not mention snacks. Therefore we are interested if snacks might not be planned opposed to meals and if that has an influence on intake. 
d. We are further interested if people with trait tendencies to plan indulgences mention snacks in the priming. To research question 1:

The Balanced Time Perspective (BTP) will be assessed using the Deviation from the Balanced Time Perspective (DBTP; Stolarski, Bitner, and Zimbardo, 2011; Zhang, Howell, and Stolarski, 2013). P. G. Zimbardo and Boyd (1999) define BTP as “an idealized mental framework that allows individuals to flexibly switch temporal frames among past, future, and present depending on situational demands, resource assessments, or personal and social appraisals.” The DBTP is calculated applying following equation: DBTP=√((oPN-ePN)^2+(oPP-ePP)^2+(oPF-ePF)^2+(oPH-ePH)^2+(oF-eF)^2 ) oPN standing for the optimal time perspective (in this case Past-Negative) and ePN for the empirical time perspective (in this case Past-Negative). For the optimal values we followed P. Zimbardo and Boyd (2014) proposal: a ‘high’ score on Past-Positive is defines as 3.67, a ‘moderately high’ score on Present-Hedonistic as 4.33 and Future as 3.69, and a ‘low’ score on Past-Negative and Present-Fatalistic as 2.10 and 1.67, respectively. A DBTP of close to zero stands for an almost perfectly balanced time perspective. On the other hand, the higher the DBTP value the more the individual’s time perspective deviates from the optimal BTP.

table.title: Influence of prospective eating plans and cognitive restraint on opportunistic snack intake
table.research_questions: We want to replicate and expand on the findings of our previous study (OSF registration: ‘Association between prospective memory of eating plans and snack intake, and influence of personality and trait tendencies to plan indulgence on this association’). This study showed that the influence of a prime for prospective memory of eating plans on opportunistic snack intake was moderated by flexible restraint, rigid restraint and cognitive restraint (measured by the Dutch Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (DEBQ)). To explore if these results are specific to thinking about foods on the same day versus the next day, we will now add an additional intervention group (‘Plan tomorrow’s food’). 1) A confirmatory moderation analysis aims to replicate previous findings. Therefore the moderating role of restraint (flexible restraint, rigid restraint and cognitive restraint (DEBQ)) on the association between priming (‘Plan today’s food’, ‘Plan tomorrow’s food’, ‘Plan today’s activities’ group) and snack intake will be assessed. 2) In an exploratory analysis time perspective, impulsiveness, emotional eating, external eating and disinhibition will be taken into account as additional moderators. To research question 1) We predict that restrained eating has a moderating role in the association between priming and intake. Participants with lower restraint (flexible, rigid and cognitive restraint) eat significantly less in the control condition compared to the intervention groups and most in the ‘Plan today’s food’ group.

1. Confirmatory analysis:
In a moderation analysis we want to investigate the association between priming of participants to think about eating plans for the rest of the day and intake, and if trait tendencies to plan indulgences moderates this interaction. We will take following possible covariates into account: eating traits (DEBQ, flexible and rigid restraint sub-scales, craving, impulsiveness), time perspective, age, gender, BMI, hunger, liking, desire to eat, perceived healthiness and mood (PANAS). First, we will correlate them with intake and only use variable as covariates which are significantly correlated with intake,

2. Exploratory analysis:
a. In an exploratory moderation analysis, we are also interested if time perspective, impulsiveness and restrained eating moderate the association between the priming and intake, as well as the moderation by trait tendencies to plan indulgences while taking a series of covariates into account. We will take the same covariates as in the confirmatory analysis into account and follow the same procedure.
b. Additionally, we want to investigate possible influences of personality and eating traits on the perceived effectiveness of planning indulgence to reduce intake of snacks.
c. During initial testing of the wording of the priming, participants did not mention snacks. Therefore we are interested if snacks might not be planned opposed to meals and if that has an influence on intake.
d. We are further interested if people with trait tendencies to plan indulgences mention snacks in the priming. To research question 1:
We hypothesis an association between priming and intake as well as a moderating role of the trait tendencies to plan indulgence. We also investigate the potential role of following covariates: eating traits (DEBQ, flexible and rigid restraint sub-scales, craving, impulsiveness), time perspective, age, gender, BMI, hunger, liking, desire to eat, perceived healthiness and mood (PANAS), if they correlate significantely with intake.
We predict that the intervention group which thinks about future eating plans will consume fewer snacks in the taste test compared to the control group which thinks about future plans in general. Zimbardo and Boyd (1999) define BTP as “an idealized mental framework that allows individuals to flexibly switch temporal frames among past, future, and present depending on situational demands, resource assessments, or personal and social appraisals.” The DBTP is calculated applying following equation: DBTP=√((oPN-ePN)^2+(oPP-ePP)^2+(oPF-ePF)^2+(oPH-ePH)^2+(oF-eF)^2 ) oPN standing for the optimal time perspective (in this case Past-Negative) and ePN for the empirical time perspective (in this case Past-Negative). report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p<.05", Text = "Figure 2 -Interaction between condition and rigid restraint on intake of sweet products. * indicates a significant difference between conditions at a certain level of cognitive restraint, and Ɨ a significant relationship between intake and restraint for a specific condition, both at a level of p<.05."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Methods: Across two pre-registered experimental studies, participants were randomly allocated to either food-related EFT or control (activity-based EFT).
Across two studies, participants were told that they would receive either a high-, low-or very-low-calorie dinner later during the day -the food EFT (vs control not related to food).
131 participants were recruited via the departmental participant pool, the staff community board and private communication at Swansea University.

Based on these exclusion criteria, data from seven participants had to be excluded (1 was vegetarian, 3 guessed the aim, and 3 had a BMI (Body Mass Index) < 18kg/m 2 ), which left data from 124 participants for analyses.

The study was approved by the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Swansea University, informed consent was obtained, and pre-registered at the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/pydvz/; DOI: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PYDVZ).

The study followed a between subject design and participants were randomly allocated to the experimental or control condition (block randomisation of 10 participants per block using http://www.random.org/).

Participants were presented with a range of snacks and were instructed to rate the sweetness, saltiness, bitterness, sourness, crunchiness, softness, liking, and healthiness of each food on a 100mm Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) to distract from the real aim of assessing intake (sensory data not otherwise used in the analysis).
Participants were invited to the study between 14.00 and 18.30 to increase consistency and the likelihood that they had eaten lunch but not dinner (similar to e.g., Higgs et al., 2008).

As can be seen in Table 1, comparable numbers of participants were in the control and experimental condition (49.2% vs 50.8%, respectively), with a similar distribution of female and male participants.
However, this hypothesised difference in snack intake would only be evident when participants were lower in (flexible, rigid and cognitive) restraint (similar to findings of study 1).
>Methods 190 participants were recruited in the same way as in study 1, which included a buffer for possible exclusion of data.
In total, 3 participants had to be excluded (1 guessed the exact aim and 2 had a BMI < 18 kg/mfoot_2 ) leaving data of 187 participants for analyses.
Participants were equally distributed between the three conditions and had similar characteristics (see Table 4).
Firstly, since participants were thinking about their own eating plans for the rest of the day of testing, these plans could not be influenced and standardised.
However, there is the possibility that participants compensated for the snack consumption by having a smaller dinner.

text.text: Objective: In our current food environment, psychosocial strategies to reduce intake and related overweight/obesity are needed.
Thinking vividly about one's personal health goal or future event (episodic future thinking; EFT) can reduce intake in the present moment.
Some people think about their future food plans instead, which might be for the same day or for a few days later.

As this has not been considered in previous research, the present studies aimed to investigate how EFT related factors (food-related EFTs and time between the current moment and the future event) influence snack intake with dietary restraint included as a moderator.
Methods: Across two pre-registered experimental studies, participants were randomly allocated to either food-related EFT or control (activity-based EFT).
Study 1 focused on food-related EFT for the present day, while study 2 also included food-related EFT for the next day.
Intake of six different sweet and savoury snacks, and dietary restraint were assessed.
Results: For study one, 124 (M age =29.7±13.2, M BMI =24.8±4.9) and for study two, 187 participants (M age =21.6±5.8, M BMI =24.0±5.1) attended the lab.
There was no significant difference in food intake following either a food-or activity-based EFT task (irrespective of duration between the present moment and the future event).
Overall, restraint did not moderate this relationship.
Conclusion: While health EFT has been shown to reduce intake in the literature, this effect has not been extended to food-related EFT here.
This might indicate the importance of content and delivery of EFT cues.

Consumers are exposed to unhealthy foods which are high in fat, salt or sugar (HFSS), such as sugarsweetened beverages, red and processed meat via media advertising (Critchlow et al., 2020), promotions and sales in supermarkets (Ejlerskov et al., 2018), and ubiquitous food outlets (Lam et al., 2021).

text.text: The combination of the nature of the products (high in HFSS) and the repeated exposure make them tempting and often high-caloric but hard to resist (Houben et al., 2012; Soetens et al., 2008).

text.text: This leads to a consumption which exceeds recommended levels, and can be related to higher mortality (Afshin et al., 2019) and overweight/obesity (Cobb et al., 2015).

text.text: Next to systemic approaches, psychological and psychosocial strategies to manage intake of these foods are needed to improve health.

In order to understand how to support people to navigate this tempting food environment, Gatzemeier et al. (2019) and Gatzemeier et al. (2024) investigated which strategies people use to manage their intake of tasty, high-caloric foods (and how effective they were perceived to be).

text.text: A wide range of strategies were identified, with those perceived as most effective and most frequently used involving future plans to indulge, e.g., postponing indulgences until the evening or planning a day to allow indulgences.
Participants pointed out that they feel that thinking about future plans to indulge can help to resist temptation in the present moment.
Indeed, previous research supports the idea of shifting the focus from a present to a future food reward to manage intake (Daniel et al., 2013).

text.text: Delay discounting (DD; also called 'delayed gratification' or 'future discounting') describes a preference for an immediate (often lesser) reward compared to a larger later reward, and is related to risky and unhealthy behaviour, e.g., drug abuse or snack intake (Odum et al., 2020).

text.text: Therefore, researchers have tried to identify interventions to reduce delay discounting as it might be an important target for behaviour interventions (Kakoschke et al., 2023).

text.text: One of these interventions is Episodic Future Thinking (EFT), the projection into or "preexperiencing" a possible future event, moment in time or state, e.g., having a lower body weight (Atance & O'Neill, 2001).

text.text: EFT seems to be a promising intervention approach as a recent metaanalysis showed a medium-sized effect of EFT on discounting in monetary and health-relevant domains (Rösch et al., 2022) by moving the attention from the immediate to the future reward.

text.text: Due to the influence of DD on healthier food choices (Kakoschke et al., 2023), some of these studies have looked at the influence of EFT not only on DD but also on food intake (e.g., Dassen et al., 2016).

text.text: Research into the use of EFT to reduce intake is relatively new and current understanding of its potential effects and mechanisms are limited.

Most studies focus on positive future events or goals, e.g., future health goals (O'Neill et al., 2016) or significant positive events in the participant's future (Mansouri et al., 2020), which are audio-recorded by the participant and then played repeatedly during an eating opportunity.
text.formatted: Most studies focus on positive future events or goals, e.g., future health goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(O'Neill et al., 2016)</ref> or significant positive events in the participant's future <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Mansouri et al., 2020)</ref>, which are audio-recorded by the participant and then played repeatedly during an eating opportunity.

text.text: These manipulations have been shown to lead to a significant reduction in consumption in the lab as well as in a food court (Daniel et al., 2013; Dassen et al., 2016; O'Neill et al., 2016; Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984; Vartanian et al., 2016).
text.formatted: These manipulations have been shown to lead to a significant reduction in consumption in the lab as well as in a food court <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Daniel et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Dassen et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">O'Neill et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Vartanian et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, the creation of the audio-recordings requires time and guidance, and listening repeatedly to the recording is less feasible if people are in groups, both of which may reduce adherence.
Additionally, these studies only looked at women and mostly young adults, so are limited in their generalisability.

Other studies have investigated the longer-term effect of EFT on intake (Mansouri et al., 2020), the use of apps to prompt listening to the manipulation when eating or deciding on a meal (Sze et al., 2015), and seeing pictures of themselves as weight-decreased and -increased (Segovia et al., 2020) not only in women, but also men, across a wider age range.
text.formatted: Other studies have investigated the longer-term effect of EFT on intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Mansouri et al., 2020)</ref>, the use of apps to prompt listening to the manipulation when eating or deciding on a meal <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Sze et al., 2015)</ref>, and seeing pictures of themselves as weight-decreased and -increased <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Segovia et al., 2020)</ref> not only in women, but also men, across a wider age range.

text.text: They found no significant effect of their EFT manipulation on energy intake and low-energy dense snack choice.
A possible limitation of these studies was that most interventions used a future event or goal as manipulation, as opposed to a future eating occasion.

In previous research, participants mentioned specifically thinking about future eating plans, indicating that this might be a more intuitive, realistic and feasible strategy than thinking about a future event or goal, and having to listen to recordings (Gatzemeier et al., 2019; Gatzemeier et al., 2024).

text.text: However, only Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984) and Vartanian et al. (2016) have investigated the effectiveness of future-eating plans on intake in the present moment, by asking participants to think about their future dinner (food EFT) and then assessing current consumption of nuts, ice cream or cookies.

(2016)</ref> have investigated the effectiveness of future-eating plans on intake in the present moment, by asking participants to think about their future dinner (food EFT) and then assessing current consumption of nuts, ice cream or cookies.

text.text: Food EFT decreased intake of snacks in these studies compared to thinking about non-food EFT or a past meal.

Taken together, previous EFT studies considering effects on food intake showed mixed results, which might be due to the heterogeneity of study design (i.e., focus on future event compared to future food intake; Ding et al., 2024).

text.text: Restrained eating indicates a conscious effort to restrict intake in order to lose weight (Stunkard & Messick, 1985).
text.formatted: Restrained eating indicates a conscious effort to restrict intake in order to lose weight <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Stunkard & Messick, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Some people use the term 'restrained eating' interchangeably with 'dietary restraint' or 'cognitive restraint', while others have different definitions for them (actual restriction of food intake vs wanting to restrict independently if they do it or not).
In many previous articles the exact definition is not clear, therefore we use such labels interchangeably here.
One suggested mechanism underpinning restrained eating is the goal conflict model of eating (Stroebe, 2022).
text.formatted: One suggested mechanism underpinning restrained eating is the goal conflict model of eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Stroebe, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: According to the model, restrained eaters have the goal of avoiding weight gain while also enjoying eating.
This creates a conflict between their goal of enjoying eating and their goal to manage their weight.
Exposure to tempting foods can increase attention to the food (Polivy & Herman, 2017) and enhance the goal of eating enjoyment, which can result in overeating (Stroebe, 2022).
text.formatted: Exposure to tempting foods can increase attention to the food <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Polivy & Herman, 2017)</ref> and enhance the goal of eating enjoyment, which can result in overeating <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Stroebe, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Prior EFT interventions shifted the focus from present to future goals (Daniel et al., 2015); one possibility is that this reduced the goal conflict and moved the focus to the longer-term goal (for restrained eaters, the weight management goal). Westenhoefer et al. (1999) broke the concept of restrained eating down into rigid (an 'all-or-nothing' approach) and flexible restraint dimensions (a more flexible approach, in which occasional 'bad' foods are allowed without feelings of guilt).

(1999)</ref> broke the concept of restrained eating down into rigid (an 'all-or-nothing' approach) and flexible restraint dimensions (a more flexible approach, in which occasional 'bad' foods are allowed without feelings of guilt).

text.text: While cognitive and rigid restraint seem to be positively related to intake, a higher flexible restraint leads to lower food intake (Westenhoefer et al., 1999).
text.formatted: While cognitive and rigid restraint seem to be positively related to intake, a higher flexible restraint leads to lower food intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Westenhoefer et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Flexible restraint seemed to overlap with the strategy highlighted by Gatzemeier et al. (2019), whereby participants allowed themselves occasional, planned indulgences, which helped them to resist the tempting food in the moment.
text.formatted: Flexible restraint seemed to overlap with the strategy highlighted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Gatzemeier et al. (2019)</ref>, whereby participants allowed themselves occasional, planned indulgences, which helped them to resist the tempting food in the moment.

text.text: While some previous EFT studies used only participants with either high or low restraint (Daniel et al., 2013; Mansouri et al., 2020; Vartanian et al., 2016), or just reported it to characterise their sample (Dassen et al., 2016), only Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984) used restraint as a potential moderating factor in their analysis.
text.formatted: While some previous EFT studies used only participants with either high or low restraint <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Daniel et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Mansouri et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Vartanian et al., 2016)</ref>, or just reported it to characterise their sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dassen et al., 2016)</ref>, only <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984)</ref> used restraint as a potential moderating factor in their analysis.

text.text: Across two studies, participants were told that they would receive either a high-, low-or very-low-calorie dinner later during the day -the food EFT (vs control not related to food).
Then they assessed intake of different nuts (study 1) or ice cream (study 2) after a milkshake pre-load.
Results were mixed, with study 1 showing that restrained and unrestrained eaters both had higher intake when anticipating a high-calorie dinner compared to control.
However, in study two, there was an interaction between restraint and condition.

These mixed results might be due to presenting healthy/savoury nuts in study 1 vs unhealthy/ sweet ice cream in study 2, and/or due to differences in restraint (rigid vs flexible; Westenhoefer et al., 1999), possibilities which were not tested further.
text.formatted: These mixed results might be due to presenting healthy/savoury nuts in study 1 vs unhealthy/ sweet ice cream in study 2, and/or due to differences in restraint (rigid vs flexible; <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Westenhoefer et al., 1999)</ref>, possibilities which were not tested further.

text.text: Taken together, a mixed picture emerges regarding the influence of EFT on intake with some clear gaps in understanding, particularly around food-specific EFTs (as identified by Gatzemeier et al., 2019; Gatzemeier et al., 2024) and the use of restraint as a highly EFT relevant moderator.
text.formatted: Taken together, a mixed picture emerges regarding the influence of EFT on intake with some clear gaps in understanding, particularly around food-specific EFTs (as identified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Gatzemeier et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Gatzemeier et al., 2024)</ref> and the use of restraint as a highly EFT relevant moderator.

text.text: Therefore, the aim of the current research was to empirically test the efficacy of food-based EFT in reducing the consumption of tempting foods in the present moment, while considering restrained eating as a potential moderator across two studies.

In summary, the limitations in previous research, which were highlighted throughout the introduction, were considered in the design of the current studies: 1) while previous research (e.g., Dassen et al., 2016; O'Neill et al., 2016; Sze et al., 2015) showed significant effects of EFTs, these were often goal-or event-related EFTs while people might more likely think about food-related EFTs (Gatzemeier et al., 2019).

text.text: Therefore, we used a food-based EFT as manipulation.
2) The manipulation was often recorded and repeatedly listened to during the meal (e.g., Daniel et al., 2013; O'Neill et al., 2016).

Therefore, a simple written task was used, which participants did not have to read continuously.
3) There were differences in the foods presented, namely, meals vs. snacks (Daniel et al., 2013; Mansouri et al., 2020), and sweet vs. savoury items (Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984).

text.text: As snacks were easier to present, the present study focused on snacks.
Sweet and savoury snacks were offered to identify if this difference might be a reason for the differences in results in the studies by Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984).

text.text: 4) Cognitive restraint is a conscious restriction of food intake to manage weight and therefore could influence intake (Herman & Mack, 1975). However Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984) found mixed results regarding the influence of restraint on the effectiveness of EFT.
text.formatted: 4) Cognitive restraint is a conscious restriction of food intake to manage weight and therefore could influence intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Herman & Mack, 1975)</ref>. <ref type="bibr">However Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984)</ref> found mixed results regarding the influence of restraint on the effectiveness of EFT.

text.text: Therefore, cognitive restraint was considered as moderator in the present studies.
Additionally, the differentiation between flexible and rigid control was considered as this might explain the mixed results.

More specifically, we aimed to address two research questions: if a food-based EFT manipulation compared to a control could reduce the intake of sweet and savoury snacks, and if restrained eating (overall, flexible and rigid) moderated this effect.

This would create a feasible and effective strategy for people to reduce their intake of tempting, but often high-caloric food, which might improve the quality of diet and help with weight management.

In study 1 we examined the influence of a food-based EFT manipulation (thinking about future food consumption later that day) compared to a control (activity-based EFT: thinking about future activities later that day) on snack intake.

The exploratory hypothesis was that participants who thought about their eating plans later that day (food-related EFT) would consume less snack-food than the control group who were asked to think about their general plans for later that day (activity-related EFT).

For our study, we used a similar protocol to studies assessing the influence of the cognitively related construct of episodic memory (EM; vividly thinking about a personal past event; Higgs et al., 2008).
text.formatted: For our study, we used a similar protocol to studies assessing the influence of the cognitively related construct of episodic memory (EM; vividly thinking about a personal past event; <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Higgs et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: 131 participants were recruited via the departmental participant pool, the staff community board and private communication at Swansea University.

Exclusion criteria were an age under 18 years and a BMI under 18 kg/m 2 , as well as food allergies or intolerances, a history of or a current diagnosed eating disorder, medications or medical conditions influencing appetite and/or taste perception, low English proficiency, being currently pregnant or breast feeding, guessing the true aim of the study, and having taken part in a previous study by the researchers.

Based on these exclusion criteria, data from seven participants had to be excluded (1 was vegetarian, 3 guessed the aim, and 3 had a BMI (Body Mass Index) < 18kg/m 2 ), which left data from 124 participants for analyses.

text.text: The control was an activity-based EFT (activities planned for the rest of the day) to be able to specify if the possible effect of the task is due to thinking about eating plans or due to future thinking.
Participants in the experimental condition were asked to write down their eating plans for the rest of the day as precisely as possible.

Participants in the control condition received the same instructions but thought about the activities they planned to do for the rest of the days, which could be anything including their eating plans (the exact wording can be found in the supplementary information A and was based on Vartanian et al., 2016).

Participants could then eat as much as they wanted as the rest would be thrown away.

To further explore the mixed results by Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984) and to cover preferences for sweet as well as savoury snacks, a range of six snacks of different textures and tastes were offered: 22g Bitsa Wispa (Cadbury, Mondelez, Birmingham, UK), 16.5g Minstrels (Mars, UK), 32g

text.text: Haribo Star Mix (HARIBO Dunhills, Pontefract, UK), 12.5g Pringles Original (Wimble Manufacturing Belgium, Mechelen, Belgium), 10g Ritz Mini Cheddars (Jacob's Bakery, Leicestershire, UK), and 4g Salted Popcorn (Tesco Stores Ltd., Cheshunt, UK).
Each participant tried the snacks in a different order, which was defined by the Qualtrics' in-built randomiser to avoid order effects.

Cognitive restraint as well as the rigid and flexible dimensions are shown to be related to intake in different ways (Niculescu et al., 2018; Olea López & Johnson, 2016; Provencher et al., 2003), but previous research into the effect of EFT on intake only looked at cognitive restraint without a differentiation between rigid and flexible control, and showed mixed results (Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984).

text.text: To test if the mixed results are due to differential effects of flexible vs rigid restraint, all three of these eating behaviour traits were included.
The Dutch Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (DEBQ; Patton et al., 1995) with 33 items has three subscales.
text.formatted: The Dutch Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (DEBQ; <ref type="bibr">Patton et al., 1995)</ref> with 33 items has three subscales.

text.text: The dietary restraint sub-scale has ten items relating to restrained eating (e.g., "When you have put on weight, do you eat less than you usually do?").
The external eating sub-scale has ten items relating to the effect of the presence of food cues in the environment (e.g., "If you see others eat do you have the desire to eat?").
The emotional eating sub-scale has thirteen items and relates to the tendency to eat in response to negative emotions (e.g., "Do you have the desire to eat when someone lets you down?").
The answers are recorded on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 'Never' to 'Very often'.
An average score for each sub-scale is calculated with higher scores indicating greater tendencies to restrained eating, eating in response to external cues or when in a negative mood, respectively.

The Cronbach's alphas were for cognitive restraint 0.91, emotional eating 0.94 and for external eating 0.81. Westenhoefer et al. (1999) further broke down the concept of restraint into flexible and rigid restraint, which is a measure based on the Three Factor Eating Questionnaire (Stunkard & Messick, 1985).

(1999)</ref> further broke down the concept of restraint into flexible and rigid restraint, which is a measure based on the Three Factor Eating Questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Stunkard & Messick, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: The twelve items of the Flexible Control sub-scale are designed to measure the flexibility of the attitude to eating, dieting and weight (e.g., "If I eat a little bit more on one day, I make up for it the next day").

The Rigid Control sub-scale consists of 16 items and relates to a rigid, black-and-white approach to eating, dieting and weight (e.g., "Do feelings of guilt about overeating help you to control your food intake?").
The average is taken for each of the sub-scales and higher scores represent a more flexible or rigid approach, respectively.
Flexible restraint had a Cronbach's alpha of 0.79 and rigid restraint of 0.77.
BMI has been shown to relate to food intake (Swinburn, Sacks, & Ravussin, 2009) and was therefore deemed important to include in the analysis.

text.text: Weight and height were measured by the researcher to calculate measured BMI with the combined Seca scale (model 778) with telescopic measuring rod (model 220).
Additionally, self-reported weight and height were requested to test potential differences between BMI with measured and self-reported weight and height.

Appetite measures (hunger, fullness, and desire to eat) were assessed before and after the bogus taste test to correct for the influence of differences in appetite before the taste test on snack intake.
Additionally, participants evaluated sensory properties to support the cover story (not used in analysis), liking and perceived healthiness of each of the snack foods.
All of these measures used a 100mm Visual Analogue Scale (VAS).

A range of psychological and eating behaviour traits were also measured as potential covariates, including, mood, and the psychological and eating behaviour traits (time perspective, impulsiveness, food craving) which have been related to intake before (AlAmmar et al., 2020; Bénard, Bellisle, et al., 2018; Bénard, Méjean, et al., 2018; Paans et al., 2019; Richard et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2017).

text.text: After consent was given, participants indicated hunger, fullness, desire to eat, and their current mood (T1).
As their main task, they were then asked to indicate their food-based or activity-based plans for the rest of the day, depending on their condition.
This was followed by the bogus taste test in which participants could eat as much or little as they wanted.
They were left alone for 10 minutes.
Then the researcher returned to see if the participant was finished with the taste test or needed more time.
Hunger, fullness, and desire to eat was assessed again after the taste test (T2).

Afterwards, they filled out a battery of questionnaires to measure demographics such as gender, age, weight and height, the psychological and eating behaviour traits, and further questions which will not be used in these analyses (but can be found on the OSF page; https://osf.io/4kmjc/?view_only=4e057daf546d4daeb4b52f50bafca200).

text.text: To identify covariates, a 2-step process was followed.
First, possible confounding factors were identified based on previous literature (see 2.1.2).

Second, demographic and/ or trait differences between the two groups (food-based vs activity-based EFT) were considered, using chi-square tests for categorical data and Mann-Whitney U for continuous data.
Significantly different variables were used as covariates.

Additional possible covariates were found by correlating appetite, demographics, and the psychological and eating behaviour traits with intake (total, sweet, or savoury) using Spearman's rho or Kruskal-Wallis test, a similar process as done by Price et al. (2017).
text.formatted: Additional possible covariates were found by correlating appetite, demographics, and the psychological and eating behaviour traits with intake (total, sweet, or savoury) using Spearman's rho or Kruskal-Wallis test, a similar process as done by <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Price et al. (2017)</ref>.

text.text: Significantly correlated variables were used as covariates.
The subsequent confirmatory and exploratory analyses were conducted:
The influence of the condition on snack intake (g) was assessed using a linear multiple regression 1.
Of interest was the influence of cognitive, flexible, and rigid restraint on the effect of condition on snack intake (g).
These associations were identified by performing moderation analyses while considering the same covariates as in the confirmatory analysis.
As we did not find a statistical difference between the conditions, we were interested if the effects of EFT on sweet and savoury snacks might have cancelled each other out.
Therefore, the multiple regression and moderation analyses were also conducted for sweet and savoury snacks separately.
Most previous studies used only sweet foods or had a mixture between sweet and savoury but did not analyse them separately.

Only Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984) ran studies with savoury 1 A multiple regression instead of an ANCOVA was used to keep the analysis consistent with the moderation analysis, which is based on multiple regression.
text.formatted: Only <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984)</ref> ran studies with savoury 1 A multiple regression instead of an ANCOVA was used to keep the analysis consistent with the moderation analysis, which is based on multiple regression.

text.text: (nuts) and sweet (ice cream) snacks, and found different results.
They reasoned that this might be due to higher affinity to sweet foods.
To replicate these results, intake of sweet and savoury snacks were analysed separately.

Correction for family wise error rate was conducted across all eating behaviour and psychological traits (see also supplemental data for results of other traits) for total, sweet and savoury snack intake separately using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure with a False Discovery Rate of 0.05 (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995).

text.text: Across cognitive, flexible and rigid restraint, as well as across the two studies, mixed results were found.
Therefore, the analyses were also conducted following the Bayesian approach (using JASP v.
0.17) to assess if the null or alternative hypotheses were more likely.
This also increased the overall robustness of the analyses.
The default priors were used as previous research also found mixed results and therefore no informative prior could be created.
For comparing the overall, sweet, and savoury snack intake between the conditions as well as for the moderations, ANCOVAs were used with the same covariates as in the frequentist analysis.
Covariates (as well as predictor and moderators for the moderation analyses) were included in the null model.

text.text: The sample was on average 29.72 years old (SD = 13.16 years) and had a mean BMI of 24.99 kg/m 2 (SD = 4.71 kg/m 2 ).
There was no difference in hunger, fullness, desire to eat, and most of the psychological and eating behaviour traits between the two conditions.

The control group had higher past positive (3.78 ± 0.60 vs 3.54 ± 0.69, p = 0.040) and lower past negative time perspective (2.85 ± 0.70 vs 3.08 ± 0.75, p = 0.047), therefore had a more positive view of their past compared to the experimental group.
Additionally, the control group found writing about their activities easier than the experimental group writing about their food plans (86.89 ± 14.64 vs 69.14 ± 28.14, p < 0.001).

text.text: First, the difference in overall snack intake between conditions was tested.

However, there was no difference in total snack intake across conditions, with our Bayesian analysis suggesting substantial support for the null hypothesis (ΔF(1,93) = 0.33, p = 0.568, ΔR2 = 0.00; BF01 = 4.186).
Additionally, the influence of condition on sweet and savoury snacks were analysed separately.

Similarly to total intake, there was no difference in the intake of sweet or savoury snacks between the conditions (sweet products: ΔF(1,106) = 2.49, ΔR2 = .01, p = .118, BF01 = 1.685; savoury products: ΔF(1,91) = 1.65, ΔR2 = .01, p = .202, BF01 = 3.191).
Our Bayesian analyses suggested anecdotal and substantial support for the null hypotheses, respectively.
Next, the moderating effect of flexible, rigid and cognitive restraint on the relationship between conditions and snack intake was assessed.

Neither overall nor savoury snack intake was moderated by (cognitive, flexible and rigid) restraint (overall: cognitive: F(1,91) = 3.37, ΔR2 = 0.03, p = 0.070; 95% CI [-18.77, 0.74]; flexible: F(1,88) = 2.87, ΔR2 = 0.03, p = 0.094, 95% CI [-5.29, 0.42]; rigid: F(1,88) = 2.24, ΔR2 = 0.02, p = 0.138, 95% CI [-4.22, 0.60]; savoury intake: cognitive: F(1,89) = 1.46, ΔR2 = 0.01, p = 0.230, 95% CI [-0.97, 4.00]).
The Bayes Factor showed no evidence for either of the hypotheses.

However, the influence of condition on sweet snack intake was moderated by cognitive (F(1,104) = 5.59, ΔR2 = 0.02, p = .020, 95% CI [ -11.42, -1.00), rigid (ΔR2 = 0.02, p = .034, 95% CI = 2.75 to 0.11,) and flexible restraint (ΔR2 = 0.02, p = .021, 95% CI [ -3.33, -0.28]).

Bayes Factors were 0.302 and 0.428 for flexible and rigid restraint, respectively, indicating anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis, while the Bayes factor for cognitive restraint indicated substantial evidence for the alternative hypothesis (BF01 = 0.290).
However, when controlled for multiple comparison, no significant moderation was maintained.

When further probed, there was a higher intake of sweet snacks in the experimental conditions, but only if the trait was low (for example of association, see Figure 2; cognitive restraint: ß = 9.80, t = 2.79, p = .006, 95% CI [2.84, 16.76]; rigid restraint: ß = 9.23, t = 2.67, p = .009, 95% CI [2.37, 16.08]; flexible restraint: ß = 9.96, t = 2.82, p = .006, 95% CI [2.95, 16.97]).

The influence of EFT on snack intake was assessed by letting participants think about food-based compared to activity-based plans prior to a bogus taste test.
Additionally, the interaction of EFT with restrained eating was explored.
Results failed to support the hypothesis, as there was no difference between the conditions in (sweet, savoury and total) intake.
In the exploratory analysis, restraint only moderated the difference in condition on sweet snack intake.
Intake increased with higher restraint, but only in the control condition, similarly to Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984).
text.formatted: Intake increased with higher restraint, but only in the control condition, similarly to <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984)</ref>.

text.text: It seems that the experimental manipulation mitigated against the increase in intake associated with restraint observed within the control condition.

While the goal-conflict model suggests that people with higher restrained might increase attention towards food if placed in front of them due to the conflict between their goal of enjoyment in the moment and the goal of weight management (Polivy & Herman, 2017; Stroebe, 2022), the EFT manipulation seem to have reduced this conflict.

text.text: This could have led to similar intakes between high and low restrained eaters.
An explanation for the equivalent results might be that most participants described their dinner in the experimental condition which was not congruent with the snacks offered in the present study.

Indeed, Fedoroff et al. (2003) suggests that attention towards and intake of food in restrained eaters might only increase if food offered and the future episode is congruent, which present findings might support.

text.text: There was a significantly higher intake of sweet products for participants in the experimental condition, when cognitive, flexible and rigid restraint were low.

These findings are in line with previous literature which found significantly higher intake in the food EFT condition compared to the control condition in unrestrained eaters (Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984).

text.text: A possible explanation might be that high restrained eaters already use considerable cognitive resources for restricting their intake, therefore, based on the counteractive control theory (Smeets et al., 2013), this may leave little resource for further cognitive activity.

text.text: However, the results should be interpreted with caution, as effects that were initially significantly did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons and explained only a very modest amount of variance.
Additionally, the influence of restraint on the effect of condition on sweet and savoury intake was exploratory and should be replicated.

Therefore, in Study 2, we aimed to replicate the results with a pre-determined focus on restrained eating -due to the significant moderating effect of restrained eating on intake in Study 1 and previous studies (e.g., Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984).

text.text: Many EFT studies let participants create cues about future events which are further in the future than in Study 1, e.g., 1 month (e.g., Dassen et al., 2016) as health goals or events are often further in the future.

text.text: However, meal plans usually span a short period of time (e.g., the same or next day).
Participants in Gatzemeier et al. (2019) talked about planning indulgences for the same evening or next weekend.
text.formatted: Participants in <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Gatzemeier et al. (2019)</ref> talked about planning indulgences for the same evening or next weekend.

text.text: This seems to indicate that they use the strategy of planning to manage temptations in the moment of temptation, not only by thinking about the same day, but also a few days ahead.
We were therefore interested in whether thinking about the meals for the next day could also influence intake in the current moment (and whether this is moderated by dietary restraint).
In Gatzemeier et al. (2019), some participants thought about their food intake later that day (similar to study 1), while others imagined the food consumed later in the week, i.e., the weekend.

text.text: Leaning on the Episodic memory (EM) literature, a second manipulation condition was added to the present study: food-based plans for the next day.
Similar to thinking about an event in one's own future (EFT), EM describes remembering and "reexperiencing" a specific event in one's own past (Tulving, 1972).
text.formatted: Similar to thinking about an event in one's own future (EFT), EM describes remembering and "reexperiencing" a specific event in one's own past <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Tulving, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: These concepts are cognitively very similar (Szpunar, 2010) and EM (writing down the last meal consumed) has been shown to lead to lower snack intake in the present moment (Higgs & Spetter, 2018; Robinson et al., 2013).

text.text: However, this effect disappeared when participants thought about the meal they consumed the day before (Higgs et al., 2008).

text.text: Therefore, the aim of study 2 was to investigate the influence of greater time being passed between the event of the EFT manipulation (here food intake) and the immediate snack intake -similarly to the EM literature (Higgs, 2002; Higgs et al., 2008) and the finding by Gatzemeier et al. (2019) that people thought not only about their meal plan of the same day, but the weekend.

text.text: Based on study 1, the first objective of study 2 was to replicate the results of study 1 that restrained eating moderates the relationship between condition and intake.
The second objective was to investigate if thinking about the meals for the next day influences snack intake.
It was predicted that the EFT condition 'same-day food EFT' would reduce intake compared to the EFT condition 'next-day food EFT' and the control condition (activity-based plans for the same day).
Additionally, it was hypothesised (pre-registered) that restrained eating would moderate the difference between conditions regarding snack intake.
Participants would eat significantly less in the control condition (activity-based EFT) compared to the experimental groups (food-based EFTs), with most eaten in the 'same-day food EFT' group.
However, this hypothesised difference in snack intake would only be evident when participants were lower in (flexible, rigid and cognitive) restraint (similar to findings of study 1).

Participants who thought about their eating plans for the next day tended to eat less of their savoury snack compared to participants who thought about their eating plans for that day, but only if they were very high in flexible restraint.

As the focus here is on restrained eating, the results of the moderation analyses with these other psychological and eating behaviour traits are in supplementary information D.
Across two experimental studies, we aimed to investigate the influence of food-based Episodic Future Thinking (EFT) on snack intake and the possible effects of restraint on this association.

However, the results did not show an effect of food-based EFT (neither same-day nor next-day EFT) on intake, contrary to our hypotheses and previous literature which looked at health-or event-based EFTs.
Also, exploratory consideration of moderation by restrained eating yielded mixed effects.
There are a range of possible explanations why no effect of food-based EFT was observed.
The effects of EFT might be very domain specific.

A food-based EFT (independent of the time until the imagined event) might increase cue reactivity and attention towards food, and therefore increased wanting of food in the moment instead of focusing on the future (Boswell & Kober, 2016).
text.formatted: A food-based EFT (independent of the time until the imagined event) might increase cue reactivity and attention towards food, and therefore increased wanting of food in the moment instead of focusing on the future <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Boswell & Kober, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, a health goal EFT reinforces that snack intake might hinder the person's desired goals (O'Neill et al., 2016), which might lead to a decrease in intake.
text.formatted: On the other hand, a health goal EFT reinforces that snack intake might hinder the person's desired goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(O'Neill et al., 2016)</ref>, which might lead to a decrease in intake.

text.text: The increased cue reactivity and attention due to the food-based EFT, might have led to disinhibited eating, because the food-based EFT might not be strong enough to override the response to the initial thought of the food.
Especially when consumption of snacks -when in front of the individual -might be established as habit.

This can lead to automatic behaviours (e.g., eating) which are uncoupled from expected outcomes (e.g., long term weight gain) and therefore cannot be influenced by future thinking of foods (see also Guthrie et al., 2013).
text.formatted: This can lead to automatic behaviours (e.g., eating) which are uncoupled from expected outcomes (e.g., long term weight gain) and therefore cannot be influenced by future thinking of foods (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Guthrie et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This might be more pronounced in individuals with low restraint since they tend not to restrict intake in order to lose weight.

As some participants in the control condition (thinking about activities planned for the rest of the day) also thought about their eating plans, this might have also increased attention towards foods.
Both conditions thinking about foods (even though to a different extend) might explain the non-significant difference in snack intake.
This is in line with Downey et al. (2025), who proposed that there is no difference in effect of EFT depending on domain (e.g., food, health, family) on delay discounting.
text.formatted: This is in line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Downey et al. (2025)</ref>, who proposed that there is no difference in effect of EFT depending on domain (e.g., food, health, family) on delay discounting.

text.text: Only food was a moderator for the effect of EFT on delay discounting, but only when no covariates were included.
However, only few studies included in this review experimentally manipulated the EFT domain as was done in the present study (Downey et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, only few studies included in this review experimentally manipulated the EFT domain as was done in the present study <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Downey et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the future, a standardised protocol for EFT studies should be developed as started by Hollis-Hansen et al. (2019) (after the beginning of both of the present studies).
text.formatted: In the future, a standardised protocol for EFT studies should be developed as started by <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hollis-Hansen et al. (2019)</ref> (after the beginning of both of the present studies).

text.text: For this, different domains (foodbased, health-based and event-based EFTs) could be manipulated and compared to find the most promising avenue.
Additionally, EFT might be more effective when only one food is offered (as in, e.g., Vartanian et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Additionally, EFT might be more effective when only one food is offered (as in, e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Vartanian et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The present study offered a variety of snacks all at the same time -different tastes (from sweet to savoury) and textures (from soft to crunchy), as might be found at buffets or parties.
Therefore, the increased consumption associated with the presence of variety may have influenced our outcome (Raynor & Vadiveloo, 2018).
text.formatted: Therefore, the increased consumption associated with the presence of variety may have influenced our outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Raynor & Vadiveloo, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: When looking at the second objective, the moderation on intake of sweet food by flexible, rigid and cognitive restraint could not be replicated in the second study, but flexible restraint interacted with condition on savoury snack intake, but only if the two manipulations (same-day and next-day foodbased plans) were compared.

A reason for this difference might be that the sample size to examine the influence of condition on intake might have provided sufficient statistical power, but not for the moderation analyses, which requires a higher sample size due to the additional interaction between predictor and moderator.
This is supported by our Bayesian analyses, which show anecdotal evidence in favour of the alternative hypotheses for most of the moderations.
Additionally, a number of very small changes were implemented between study 1 and 2 such as exchange of the brand of popcorn and sweets to accommodate vegetarians.
This could have impacted the comparability of the results.
Therefore, the findings should be interpreted with caution.
To decrease these limitations, more participants should be recruited to sufficiently power a moderation analysis and consistent snacks offered.
Methodological differences between previous and present studies might explain the differences in findings.
This shows the impact of the formulation (e.g., health goal vs food-based EFT) and presentation of the EFT (once vs repeated during meal) on the efficacy of EFT.

While research found a significant effect of EFT on intake (Ding et al., 2024), it might not be easily implemented in everyday life in a range of situations (e.g., not only at home, but also when having a meal out with friends).
text.formatted: While research found a significant effect of EFT on intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Ding et al., 2024)</ref>, it might not be easily implemented in everyday life in a range of situations (e.g., not only at home, but also when having a meal out with friends).

text.text: When eating out of home with friends and family, which is associated with higher energy intake (Lachat et al., 2012), it might not be feasible to listen repeatedly to a cue.
text.formatted: When eating out of home with friends and family, which is associated with higher energy intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Lachat et al., 2012)</ref>, it might not be feasible to listen repeatedly to a cue.

text.text: Therefore, future research should focus on identifying presentations which are easy to adopt in day-to-day life and subjectively effective.
This can increase acceptance and implementation long-term (Bos et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This can increase acceptance and implementation long-term <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bos et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: EFT could be an easy and cost-effective tool to manage intake with cues being created with the help of healthcare professionals, apps or websites.
A few limitations of the current study must be noted.
Firstly, since participants were thinking about their own eating plans for the rest of the day of testing, these plans could not be influenced and standardised.
Though more realistic, there might be many factors influencing the results which were not directly measured.

The future foods may have differed in (1) calorie content, which was shown to influence intake (Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984), (2) in flavour, possibly incongruent to the flavour of the snacks offered (Fedoroff et al., 2003), and (3) amount, since it was all the food until they went to bed without any further specification (meals vs. snack).
text.formatted: The future foods may have differed in (1) calorie content, which was shown to influence intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Tomarken & Kirschenbaum, 1984)</ref>, (2) in flavour, possibly incongruent to the flavour of the snacks offered <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fedoroff et al., 2003)</ref>, and (3) amount, since it was all the food until they went to bed without any further specification (meals vs. snack).

text.text: Future studies should either offer or pretend to offer a standardised meal, similar to EM studies (Higgs, 2002; Higgs & Jones, 2013) and Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984).
text.formatted: Future studies should either offer or pretend to offer a standardised meal, similar to EM studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Higgs, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Higgs & Jones, 2013)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Tomarken and Kirschenbaum (1984)</ref>.

text.text: Secondly, some people ate all the snacks offered within the laboratory, which might have led to a ceiling effect.
More food could be offered to identify greater differences between intakes.
Thirdly, the presented studies only measured intake immediately after the experimental manipulation.
However, there is the possibility that participants compensated for the snack consumption by having a smaller dinner.

In previous research participants mentioned to schedule indulgences for the weekend (Gatzemeier et al., 2019), so they might have made a plan whilst within our laboratory to eat fewer tempting foods later to balance the snack intake during the study.
text.formatted: In previous research participants mentioned to schedule indulgences for the weekend <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Gatzemeier et al., 2019)</ref>, so they might have made a plan whilst within our laboratory to eat fewer tempting foods later to balance the snack intake during the study.

text.text: This planned compensation could be examined by letting participants keep a food diary for a week (Johnson, 2002; Rutishauser, 2005).
text.formatted: This planned compensation could be examined by letting participants keep a food diary for a week <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Johnson, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Rutishauser, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Fourthly, a range of analyses were conducted to investigate the influence of different psychological and eating behaviour traits on the effect of the EFT on snack intake.
Additionally, the results from study 1 and 2 were inconsistent.
Therefore, the results should be interpreted with caution as these were exploratory and might be underpowered.
Future research should run the study again with a larger sample size and focussing on restrained eating to reduce the risk of type II and I errors, respectively.

Fifthly, while covariates were determined via a two-step process and the use of a correlation matrix -a similar process as has been done previously (e.g., Price et al., 2017) -there is an increased risk of overfitting which is acknowledged.
text.formatted: Fifthly, while covariates were determined via a two-step process and the use of a correlation matrix -a similar process as has been done previously (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Price et al., 2017)</ref> -there is an increased risk of overfitting which is acknowledged.

text.text: Therefore, future studies should consider using other methods to identify covariates as suggested by Sauer et al. (2013).
text.formatted: Therefore, future studies should consider using other methods to identify covariates as suggested by <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Sauer et al. (2013)</ref>.

text.text: Lastly, the participants in both studies were young (study 1: M=30 years and study 2: M=22 years) and mostly university students.
Age is shown to influence snack intake (Si Hassen et al., 2018) as well as EFT (Schacter et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Age is shown to influence snack intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Si Hassen et al., 2018)</ref> as well as EFT <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Schacter et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the results cannot be generalised and are likely only representing younger adults.
To conclude, no difference between food-based (same-day and next-day) and activity-based EFTs on snack intake was found.
This might be because food-based EFTs do not necessarily align with health goals and are not excluding current intake.
Therefore, health-based EFTs might be more effective.
When restraint was considered, results were mixed, possibly due to small sample sizes.
Therefore, the study should be replicated with larger sample sizes.
